passage:
I'm Gurpreet. I sit next to Hafsa in the hostel study room, so I saw how it started.
On Tuesday Hafsa got a text: Your scholarship KYC is pending. Update in 2 hrs or payment stops, with a link. She didn't tap it. She frowned, opened the university portal herself, and found nothing pending.
Then she did something I wouldn't have thought of. She took a screenshot, crossed out the link in red, and posted it in our class group: Fake. Don't click. Check the portal directly. She reported the number on the cybercrime portal too, and sent the same screenshot to her family group with a voice note in Urdu for her grandmother.
By evening, three people in our class said they had got it too. I forwarded Hafsa's warning to my Nani. She called me that night. She had received a similar message about her pension and hadn't known what to do.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa check whether her KYC was pending?
qa.a: She opened the university portal herself and found nothing pending.

qa.q: What does Hafsa's frown suggest when the text arrived?
qa.a: It suggests she felt suspicious of the urgent deadline and link rather than panicked.

qa.q: Which of Hafsa's steps protected the most people?
qa.a: Posting a marked screenshot with a clear warning to the class and family groups, including a voice note for her grandmother, spread the alert to people less used to such tricks.

qa.q: What was it like for Gurpreet's Nani to get the warning?
qa.a: Nani was relieved, having received a similar pension message without knowing what to do.

grounding: A student who spots a fake scholarship message checks the official portal, reports it and warns her class and family, and the warning reaches an older relative in time.

passage:
Monday. Damini, three months into her first job, got an email that seemed to come from the office IT team: Mailbox full. Log in here within 24 hours. The sender's address ended in a strange domain. She reported it with the phishing button and forgot about it.
Wednesday. At lunch, Devika from accounts, who is close to retirement and still prints her emails, mentioned a mailbox-full warning she planned to deal with after tea. Damini put down her fork. "Can I look at it with you first?" Same strange domain. They reported it together, and Damini posted a short note in the team chat: Fake IT emails going around. Check the sender. When in doubt, call IT on the extension.
Friday. IT sent an office-wide alert. Four people had received the email; nobody had logged in. Devika stopped by Damini's desk with a box of homemade laddoos. "For the warning," she said.

qa.q: What did the fake email tell Damini to do?
qa.a: It said Mailbox full. Log in here within 24 hours.

qa.q: Why did Damini put down her fork at lunch?
qa.a: She was alarmed, recognising the fake email she had reported and worried Devika would log in after tea.

qa.q: What made Damini's warning in the team chat useful?
qa.a: It was short and practical: check the sender, and when in doubt call IT on the extension, so less experienced email users knew exactly what to do.

qa.q: How did Devika feel about Damini's help?
qa.a: Devika felt grateful, bringing homemade laddoos to thank Damini for the warning.

grounding: A young employee reports a phishing email, spots it again in Devika's inbox and warns the whole team, so no one logs in.

passage:
Ramesh, you rolled your eyes when I posted that scam warning in the family group. Let your Maria Aunty tell you why I do it.
When I was twenty, at college in Mangalore, I got an SMS: "Your bank account will be blocked today. Click to update KYC." It looked exactly like our bank's messages. I nearly clicked. Then I noticed the sender was a normal mobile number, and the link was misspelt.
I didn't just delete it. I rang the bank's official number, and they said it was fake. Then I thought of my grandfather, who had just learned to use a mobile. So I called home and told everyone.
Two days later, Grandpa got the same message. He remembered my call and didn't click. Our neighbour, who nobody warned, lost her pension that week.
That's why I post warnings, Ramesh. Someone less used to phones might be reading.

qa.q: What did young Maria notice about the SMS?
qa.a: She noticed the sender was a normal mobile number, and the link was misspelt.

qa.q: How did young Maria feel when she thought of her grandfather?
qa.a: She felt worried and protective, knowing he had just learned to use a mobile and could easily be fooled.

qa.q: What turning point in the story showed why warning others matters?
qa.a: Her grandfather got the same message two days later and didn't click, while a neighbour who wasn't warned lost her pension.

qa.q: How might Maria's grandfather have felt when he recognised the message?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and grateful that Maria had warned the family.

grounding: An aunt recalls spotting a phishing message as a student, reporting it and warning her family, which protected her grandfather.

passage:
It was the last hour before the scholarship form deadline, and the class chat group was chaos. Everyone was rushing.
Then a message appeared from an unknown number: "Official scholarship portal extended! Submit here + pay ₹199 verification fee." A link. Twenty people reacted with thumbs up.
Charu stared at it. The link ended in something strange, not the government domain. And real scholarship forms never asked for a fee.
Anjali, beside her in the library, was already typing her bank details. "Charu, quick, it's closing!"
"Wait." Charu grabbed her wrist gently. "Look at the link. It's fake."
Anjali stopped, eyes wide.
Charu posted in the group: "Don't click that link. It's not the official portal. Real scholarships don't charge fees. Use the government site directly." She reported the number, then forwarded the warning to her mother's family group, where her aunts were always forwarding things.
Three people replied, "Thank you, I almost paid."

qa.q: How much was the fake verification fee?
qa.a: ₹199 verification fee.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when she saw the link?
qa.a: Charu felt suspicious and alert, doubting the message because the link wasn't the government domain.

qa.q: What did Charu do to protect others?
qa.a: She stopped Anjali, warned the class group, reported the number, and forwarded the warning to her mother's family group.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel when Charu stopped her?
qa.a: Anjali felt shocked and relieved, her eyes wide as she realised she had nearly given her bank details.

grounding: It shows a student spotting a phishing link under deadline pressure, reporting it and warning her class and older relatives.

passage:
On Sunday morning, Leela got an SMS on her phone in the Bengaluru flat: "Dear customer, your electricity will be disconnected tonight at 9:30 pm due to unpaid bill. Call this officer immediately." A mobile number.
She had paid her bill last week. She checked the electricity board's official app: no dues. The number didn't match the board's helpline. Fake.
She almost deleted it. Then she thought of the older residents in her building, the ones who kept their bills in files and phoned the board for everything.
She posted a screenshot in the residents' group: "Scam alert! Don't call this number. Check the official app or the board's helpline instead."
Ten minutes later, Ramesh Uncle from the ground floor knocked on her door, holding his phone. "Beta, I was just about to call them. They'd have asked for my card, na?"
"Probably, Uncle." Leela showed him how to check his bill on the official app.

qa.q: What time did the SMS say the electricity would be disconnected?
qa.a: Tonight at 9:30 pm.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when she thought of the older residents?
qa.a: Leela felt concerned and protective, worried that people less used to digital tricks might be fooled.

qa.q: What did Leela do that protected others?
qa.a: She posted a scam alert in the residents' group and showed Ramesh Uncle how to check his bill on the official app.

qa.q: How did Ramesh Uncle feel when he came to Leela's door?
qa.a: Ramesh Uncle felt relieved and grateful, having nearly called the number before seeing her warning.

grounding: It shows a young adult spotting a phishing SMS, reporting it and warning her building, protecting an older neighbour.

passage:
"Irfan, did you get this?" Vidya held out her phone in the library corridor. "Scholarship refund pending. Click to verify your bank details."
"Yeah, this morning. I nearly clicked. Looked official."
"Look at the sender. It's a random ten-digit number. And the link is misspelled: scholarsip."
"Huh. Okay, that's fake."
"I'm reporting it to the college IT cell. And I'm posting in the class group."
"Everyone will just ignore it."
"Maybe. But Tenzin told me her mother almost paid a refund fee last year. Some people won't spot it."
Irfan went quiet. "My Nani forwards everything. She'd click this in a second."
"Then send it to your family group too. With a screenshot, so she can see what it looks like."
"What do I even say?"
"Keep it simple. Fake message going around. Don't click. If unsure, call me."
Irfan was already typing. "Done. Nani replied with a thumbs-up."

qa.q: How was the link misspelled?
qa.a: It said scholarsip.

qa.q: What seems to motivate Vidya to warn everyone?
qa.a: Vidya feels concerned for people less used to these tricks, like Tenzin's mother, and wants to protect them early.

qa.q: What makes a good warning message, as Vidya suggests?
qa.a: Something short and clear with a screenshot: fake message going around, don't click, if unsure call me.

qa.q: Why might Irfan's Nani be helped by the warning?
qa.a: Nani forwards everything and might click in a second, so a simple screenshot from Irfan helps her recognise the trick and feel safe asking.

grounding: Shows a student who spots a suspicious message, reports it and warns classmates and family, protecting those less used to digital tricks.
